title: Practical Action

paragraphs.text: In the developing world, although the role of transport is acknowledged by national policy makers to be a positive catalyst for progress, these policy makers often lack an understanding of the particular transport problems faced by poor rural and urban communities. Priority is usually given to developing large-scale road systems for motor traffic, encouraging the use of private motorised vehicles. Developments like this do not meet the transport needs of the poor, especially those in rural areas, where most of the villages are situated far away from the vehicular roads, and rural townships.

In these rural areas travel usually falls into two distinct categories: on-farm and off-farm. Most of the on-farm or ‘on-village’ tasks are for domestic subsistence purposes, such as the gathering of firewood and collecting water, with some activities, such as transporting farm implements, seeds and fertilisers to the fields, being indirectly related to economic purposes. Off-farm travel or ‘village travel’ is usually done to gain access to schools, health centres, shops and public offices, and for socially-related travel. Often, economic-related travel, such as going to the markets or getting to the nearest navigable road, falls into the category of off-farm or village travel. Most non-economic travel is carried out by women and children, although generally men, women and children all travel on foot, and either carry goods on their heads or use animals.

Practical Action, founded in 1966, is a charity that works directly in four regions of the developing world: Latin America, East Africa, Southern Africa and South Asia. The organisation links up with rural and urban communities, transport service providers and local and national authorities. It does this in order to analyse needs and explore the options that could help make a real impact on lives and livelihoods in rural communities in two main ways: by improving people’s access to markets and by reducing the time spent by women and children on daily tasks.

As well as developing new ideas, Practical Action also commissions and participates in research, and works with international transport networks to ensure that its projects are really meeting local needs.

Practical Action has a unique approach to development – the organisation doesn’t start with technology, but with people. The tools may be simple or sophisticated, but to provide long-term, appropriate and practical answers, the organisers feel they must be firmly in the hands of local people who shape technology and control it for themselves.

One part of this approach includes the development of Intermediate Means of Transport or IMTs. These are transport devices that come between walking and conventional motor vehicles, such as ox and donkey carts, handcarts and wheelbarrows, some of which help people make more effective use of animals for transporting heavy loads.
Case Study: The Practical Action Bicycle Ambulance

In the flat plains of Nepal, poor people cannot reach medical care when they need it. People may be dying and there is no way to help them. Yet even in the poorest villages, people have bicycles — but how do you take a person on a bicycle when they are sick?

At the time, Practical Action was already working with the villagers to build bicycle trailers to take goods to market. The next step was to adapt them to become ‘ambulances’. Practical Action provided the expertise and the villagers themselves provided the hard work.

The Practical Action bicycle trailer is now being trialled in a number of communities in the terai (plains) of Nepal, where it is proving most successful. Local, specific adaptations to the basic technology ensure maximum efficiency, durability and appropriateness for the community, use and location.

The two-wheeled trailer is made from moulded metal, with standard rubber-tyred wheels. The ‘bed’ section is padded with cushions to make the patient comfortable, while the ‘seat’ section allows a family member to attend to the patient during transit.

A dedicated bicycle is needed to pull the ambulance trailer, so that other community members do not need to go without the bicycles they depend on in their daily lives. A joining mechanism allows for easy removal and attachment.

In response to user comments, a cover has been designed that can be added to give protection against bad weather to the patient and the person accompanying them. (The Nepal rainy season is June and July.) Made of treated cotton, the cover is durable and waterproof.
The total cost of a whole bicycle ambulance is £150 — but to people who need it, it is priceless.
